data.title: Asian markets slip as tech selloff deepens; oil prices remain elevated
data.description:
Asian markets were mostly lower on Tuesday as investors weighed elevated oil prices, geopolitical tensions, and weakness in technology stocks, particularly semiconductors, amid growing concerns over the safety of AI development.

Wall Street closed lower Monday as investors weighed AI developments and monitored oil prices following a sharp rally. The Dow fell 0.2%, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.5%.

U.S. stock futures were lower on Tuesday, with Dow futures down 0.27%, S&P 500 futures falling 0.14% and Nasdaq futures declining 0.10%.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.43%, while the yen weakened 0.50% against the dollar.

China’s Shanghai Composite slipped 0.10% and touched a three-month low at the start of the day. The offshore yuan held its decline around 6.71 per dollar on Tuesday, staying off its recent more than three-year high. China retail sales miss expectations, while urban unemployment hits 5.3%. China’s industrial production grew 5.2% Y/Y in August.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index fell 0.23%, as investors remained cautious ahead of key economic and monetary policy developments. 

South Korea’s Kospi dropped 0.32%.

India’s Sensex gained 0.32%. The Indian rupee fell to around 95.8 per dollar, remaining near seven-week lows as persistent oil price gains.

Australia’s ASX 200 declined 0.81%, extending weakness in the regional market.

data.title: Sysco prices 12.3M-share offering at $81 each to help finance Jetro purchase
data.description:
• Sysco Corporation (SYY) priced its offering of ~12.34M shares of its common stock at a price to public of $81 a piece, according to a company statement on Tuesday.
  • Sysco (SYY) expects the offering to close September 16, and plans to use net proceeds to finance a portion of consideration for the pending acquisition of Jetro Restaurant Depot.
  • Underwriters have a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional $150M of shares of common stock at the same price as the other shares, solely to cover overallotments, if any.
  • Goldman Sachs and TD Securities are lead bookrunners; BofA Securities, J.P. Morgan Securities, and Wells Fargo Securities are also bookrunning managers.
  • The stock eased 2.2% in extended trading on Monday.

data.title: Broadcom CEO dismisses AI slowdown concerns, stands by long-term revenue goals
data.description:
Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan dismissed fears that a potential slowdown in frontier AI model development would impact the company, telling CNBC that the chipmaker remains committed to its long-term revenue targets.

Tan’s comments came as investors were rattled by Anthropic (ANTHRO) CEO Dario Amodei’s weekend essay advocating for a moderation in the pace of model development. Amodei’s message, which received support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, prompted investors in AI infrastructure providers to reconsider their expectations for compute demand during Monday’s session.

Shares of Broadcom — whose custom-chip business counts Anthropic as one of its most important customers — fell 4.8%. A broad basket of chip stocks, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOX), fell 5.6%. The stocks of companies selling other data-center components were also hit hard.

“No, not in the least,” Tan said, when Jim Cramer asked whether anything in the AI slowdown debate has caused him to reconsider Broadcom’s fiscal 2027 and 2028 AI semiconductor forecasts. “We see the demand for compute infrastructure, for AI development or AI frontier models, and inference for the products that they feed to the world, as continuing to be very strong and, I believe, very durable.”

Tan also said Anthropic is on track to become Broadcom’s largest custom chip customer in 2027 and sustain that designation in 2028 — illustrating why Broadcom (AVGO) investors are so sensitive to Amodei’s commentary. Google has historically been considered Broadcom’s biggest custom customer, co-designing Google’s (GOOG) (GOOGL) tensor processing units.

In Monday’s CNBC interview, Tan was particularly optimistic about demand for inference, the day-to-day usage of AI models after they’ve been trained.

“I don’t know about training, but when you want to productize inference, I see it continuing to be very, very strong,” Tan said.

data.title: China retail sales miss expectations, while urban unemployment hits 5.3%
data.description:
• China’s retail sales growth slowed to 0.4% Y/Y in August 2026 from 0.6% in July, missing market expectations of 0.8%.
  • Auto sales fell 18.5%, while furniture, building materials, and gold and silver jewelry sales declined 7.9%, 11.8%, and 17.5%, respectively. Excluding autos, retail sales grew 2.5%.
  • Meanwhile, China’s surveyed urban unemployment rate rose to 5.3% from 5.2% in July, above the 5.2% expected and the highest since March. The rate among migrant workers increased to 5.2% from 5.1%.
  • From January to August, retail sales rose 1.1% year-on-year, while the average urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2%, unchanged from the first seven months.

data.title: EPA to roll back Biden-era limits on power plant emissions
data.description:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Monday it will repeal some carbon dioxide emission rules for power plants, the latest step in the Trump administration's broader effort to curb the agency's role in regulating climate change.

Under the final rule announced at the G-20 summit for energy ministers in Houston, the EPA is ending a Biden-era mandate requiring existing and future fossil fuel-fired power plants to dramatically curb their emissions in the coming decades through the use of specific technologies, including carbon capture and storage.

The EPA also proposed a new rule repealing the federal finding that greenhouse gases from power plants specifically are a significant source of air pollution, effectively a separate endangerment finding for power plants under the Clean Air Act after the agency acted in February to rescind the Obama-era endangerment finding, which classifies six greenhouse gases as a threat to public health and welfare.

The administration's rule changes earlier this year focused on the auto sector and tailpipe emissions, not the power industry.

"Today's proposal states the Clean Air Act does not give us the authority to regulate power plant emissions based on climate change," EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said at the G-20 meeting. "At EPA, we follow a very simple principle: If Congress didn't authorize it, EPA shouldn't be doing it."

Energy industry groups celebrated the rollback, while environmentalists and some former EPA officials criticized the repeal and warned that its economic and environmental fallout could be significant.

data.title: Chevron CEO Wirth, other U.S. oil executives warn global fuel crisis has arrived
data.description:
Trump administration officials have said the current oil market disruption is temporary, but Chevron's (CVX) Mike Wirth and other industry executives are warning global supplies are running low, with no respite in sight.

Commercial fuel stocks around the world have been depleting for more than six months, and strategic crude reserves cannot be tapped much further, oil executives say, after attacks last week shut down a crucial crude pipeline in Saudi Arabia that bypassed the Strait of Hormuz, stranding an estimated 2.5M bbl/day at least from an already tight global oil market.

"All these mechanisms helped to mitigate the price and supply risk," Chevron (CVX) CEO Mike Wirth said Friday at an energy conference in Austin, Texas, according to The Wall Street Journal. "Those have largely now played out, and we don't have nearly the buffers in the system that we did when [the Middle East war] began."

"It's harder ​to envision a scenario where prices soften and quickly," Wirth said. "I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months."

U.S. retail diesel prices have skyrocketed to a record $6.23/gal, and gasoline prices, which had slipped below $4 during the summer, have bounced to $4.32/gal, and WSJ reported that some CEOs and energy advisers are growing alarmed as the Middle East conflict has picked up again, with ships and energy infrastructure being targeted in both directions.

"The advantage in most negotiations usually goes to the side that has time on their side and is willing to be patient," and Iran is "willing to suffer," Quantum Capital Group CEO Wil VanLoh said at the Austin conference. "Their people have already suffered a lot for many decades."

Analysts say China is in part helping to exacerbate the global supply pinch, resuming bigger purchases from international suppliers after relying for months on its own stockpiles of crude for nearly half of its daily consumption, which had provided a reprieve for oil markets.

Crude oil futures settled higher Monday on mounting worries about energy supplies following new ‌strikes on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and attacks on ships in the Middle East.

But prices eased off early highs, led by diesel, after President Trump said Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop attacks on each other's energy facilities, although neither country has independently said they are holding to the deal.

Ukraine President Zelenskyy said his country would be willing to suspend its strikes "if our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes... Ukraine is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement."

Front-month Nymex crude (CL1:COM) for October delivery gained 1.3% to $101.39/bbl, front-month Brent crude (CO1:COM) for November delivery added 1% to $105.68/bbl, and front-month Nymex October natural gas (NG1:COM) climbed 2.3% to $2.896/MMBtu.
